chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Asbat, from Al-A'ala ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two Imams (peace be upon them), who said:
I said, 'We see a man who has worship, striving, and humility, but he does not speak with the Truth (Wilayah); will that benefit him in any way?'

He said, 'O Abu Muhammad! The example of the People of the Household is like the example of a household among the Children of Israel. No one from them would strive for forty nights and supplicate except that he would be answered.'

And indeed, a man from them strived for forty nights, then supplicated, but he was not answered. So he came to Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him), complaining to him of what he was in, and asked him for supplication.

So Isa purified himself and prayed, then supplicated to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed to him: 'O Isa! My servant came to me from other than the door through which I am approached.'
'He supplicated to me, and in his heart was doubt about you. So even if he were to supplicate to me until his neck breaks and his fingers scatter, I will not answer him.'
He said, 'So Isa (peace be upon him) turned towards him and said, 'You supplicate to your Lord while you are in doubt about His Prophet?''
So he said, 'O Spirit of Allah and His Word! It has been, by Allah, what you said. So supplicate to Allah for me that He removes it from me.'
So Isa (peace be upon him) supplicated for him, and Allah turned to him (with forgiveness) and accepted from him, and he came to be within the limit of the People of the Household.

key_terms.أَهْلُ الْبَيْتِ: The People of the Household (Ahl al-Bayt)
key_terms.الْبَابُ: The door/channel of approach to God, referring to Wilayah

ai.seo_question: Why did a man's prolonged worship and supplication fail to be answered in the story of the Children of Israel?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* underscores the Shia doctrine that sincere belief in the *Wilayah* of the Imams is a prerequisite for the acceptance of worship, illustrating that ritual devotion without theological certainty is insufficient. The narrative draws a parallel between the Children of Israel and the Ahl al-Bayt, emphasizing that doubt (*shakk*) in the divinely appointed guide nullifies the efficacy of supplication, a principle central to Usuli scholarship. It serves as a foundational text for understanding the interconnection between creed (*aqidah*) and practice (*fiqh*) in Shia jurisprudence.
